query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A short high-temperature oxidation pre-treatment applied to CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy surfaces will form a stable, thin oxide layer that, in situ during sliding across temperatures from room temperature to 800 °C, consistently lowers the friction coefficient and wear rate compared to untreated alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy in its untreated, single-phase condition, known to exhibit higher friction and wear over a wide temperature range.
generation.intervention: Apply a brief high-temperature oxidation pre-treatment (e.g., heating at ≈800 °C for a few minutes in a controlled, mildly oxidizing atmosphere) to develop a protective oxide layer on the alloy's surface.
generation.conditions: Sliding experiments performed from room temperature (≈25 °C) to 800 °C, under varying loads (approximately 10–20 N) and in air or mildly oxidizing environmental conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: A pre-formed, stable, and continuous thin oxide film that acts as an in situ tribo-oxide during sliding.
generation.mechanism: The initial oxidation pre-treatment creates a lubricious oxide layer that reduces interfacial shear strength and inhibits adhesive wear. This layer resists degradation under varying temperatures and loads, thereby stabilizing the friction interface and reducing material loss.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated CoCrFeNi alloy is expected to exhibit a friction coefficient below approximately 0.3 and at least a 50% reduction in wear rate relative to untreated samples, consistently across the full temperature range up to 800 °C.
generation.baseline: Untreated CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy samples undergoing identical sliding tests under the same environmental, load, and temperature conditions.
generation.boundary: Effective within the sliding temperature range of 25 °C to 800 °C, under loads up to about 20 N and in air or mildly oxidizing environments. Deviations from these conditions may alter the oxide layer stability and thus the tribological behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvements (e.g., the exact friction coefficient value and percentage reduction in wear rate) are estimated from analogous studies and require verification through systematic experimentation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeNi alloy coupons. One set is subjected to the high-temperature oxidation pre-treatment (≈800 °C for a few minutes in a controlled atmosphere), while the other set is left untreated. Conduct pin-on-disk sliding wear tests at multiple temperatures (e.g., 25 °C, 300 °C, 600 °C, and 800 °C) and under varied loads (e.g., 10 N and 20 N) in air or a mildly oxidizing environment.
measurements: Steady-state friction coefficient during sliding at each temperature and load.
Specific wear rate determined from wear scar dimensions or volume loss.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the pre-treated samples do not show a significantly lower friction coefficient (i.e., remain above ≈0.3) and do not achieve at least a 50% lower wear rate compared to the untreated samples at any of the testing conditions.

cited_evidence.text: This is also consistent with the previous friction coefficient data and specific wear rate data. The friction coefficient of FG sample is small, and the specific wear rate is low. Under high normal load, with the increase of sliding speed, the main wear mechanisms of the two samples are adhesive wear, oxidative wear, and plastic deformation. Compared with low loading, the phenomena of wear debris, glaze layers, and oxide layers occurred earlier. This indicates that both samples are more prone to oxidation friction under the high normal load. The oxide layer acts as a lubricating layer, resulting in a reduced coefficient of friction on the worn surface. Therefore, in the friction coefficient curve, the friction coefficient of both samples under high normal load conditions is smaller than that of under low normal load. However, the formation of the oxide layer is accompanied by the occurrence of oxidative wear, which leads to the accumulation of wear volume and the increase of specific wear rate. At this point, the oxide layer formed on the FG sample is more resistant to rupture. Therefore, the FG sample shows good wear resistance.

In the present study, the tribological properties of different grain sizes CoCrFeMnNi HEAs were systematically analyzed based on sliding experiments and worn surface morphology characterization under different sliding speeds and normal loads. The results can be summarized as follows: Under the normal low load and low sliding speed, the main wear mechanism of FG and CG samples is adhesive wear. With the increase in sliding speed, the wear mechanisms are adhesive wear and oxidation wear. However, the material of CG is easy to soften under the action of friction heat during high sliding speed, and the oxide layer formed is easy to fracture. Under the normal high load, the wear mechanisms of FG and CG samples are mainly adhesive wear, oxidation wear, and plastic deformation with the increase of sliding speed. The oxidation layer formed on CG sample has many cracks, and the wear surface of CG sample also has plastic deformation, resulting in an increase in friction coefficient and specific wear rate and a decrease in wear resistance. Therefore, under high load and low load, FG sample has good wear resistance due to its high surface strength.

decision.trend: Early tribological studies on related CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloys (PMC7311485, 2020) demonstrated that refining grains and forming ultra-fine near-surface layers can lower friction and wear, though testing largely occurred near room temperature and in controlled atmospheres. Subsequent work (PMC8470387, 2021) introduced tungsten additions to AlCoCrFeNi coatings to boost wear resistance up to ~800 °C, highlighting the role of in situ oxide formation, but it did not pinpoint solutions for CoCrFeNi without alloying. More recently, a study on CoCrFeMnNi (PMC9960858, 2023) revealed that grain-size control can improve oxidation and deformation resistance, but did not address the full range to 800 °C. Meanwhile, complex concentrated alloys with hierarchical microstructures can achieve superb tribological stability from room temperature to 800 °C (PMC10241162, 2023). Nevertheless, a resilient, single-intervention strategy for CoCrFeNi specifically over 20–800 °C remains elusive.
decision.unsolved: Despite evidence that microstructure control, surface oxide formation, and advanced coatings can reduce friction and wear at high temperatures, there is no established method to maintain such performance in CoCrFeNi over the entire range from room temperature to 800 °C under various loads and environments. The exact interplay between near-surface transformations, oxidation, and tribofilm stability in this specific alloy system still lacks clarity.
decision.lever: Implement a short high-temperature oxidation pre-treatment in controlled atmospheres (e.g., ~800 °C for minutes) to form a stable, thin oxide layer on the CoCrFeNi surface, enabling an in situ tribo-oxide film that maintains low friction from ambient to 800 °C across a range of loads and air or controlled environments.
decision.why: Prior work (e.g., PMC8470387, PMC10241162) indicates that stable oxide or glaze layers can significantly reduce friction and wear under high-temperature sliding. By generating such a protective layer on CoCrFeNi without altering bulk composition, this approach matches the single-intervention requirement and avoids routine alloying. The hypothesized outcome is a consistently low friction coefficient (<0.3) and reduced wear (≥50% lower mass loss) relative to untreated CoCrFeNi, for loads up to ~10–20 N and temperatures up to 800 °C, in both air and mildly oxidizing environments. A controlled experiment would subject identical CoCrFeNi coupons (with and without the oxidation pre-treatment) to pin-on-disk wear tests at incremental temperatures (25, 300, 600, 800 °C). Observation of no significant improvement in friction and wear performance—e.g., a friction coefficient remaining above 0.5 or comparable wear to the untreated reference—would falsify the hypothesis.
